OPHTHALMIC__Red Eye:
A red eye is common and usually benign, but a handful of causes threaten sight or life.
  • The job at the front door is to separate the dangerous red eye from simple conjunctivitis. Ask three questions: is there pain (a truly painful red eye is never “just conjunctivitis”), is vision reduced, and is there photophobia?
  • Red flags are acute angle-closure glaucoma (red painful eye + haloes + a fixed mid-dilated pupil + vomiting) (see acute angle-closure glaucoma), microbial keratitis / corneal ulcer (contact-lens wearers, and the HSV dendritic ulcer) (see HSV keratitis), anterior uveitis (photophobia + ciliary flush + small pupil) (see uveitis / iritis), and scleritis (severe boring pain) (see scleritis / episcleritis).
  • A chemical burn or penetrating trauma, or orbital cellulitis (proptosis + restricted movements + fever) (see proptosis), are emergencies. Most other red eyes are conjunctivitis (see bacterial, allergic) or a harmless subconjunctival haemorrhage.
🚨A painful red eye with reduced vision or photophobia is an emergency until proven otherwise. Do not prescribe chloramphenicol and send away. Acute angle-closure glaucoma — a hard, red, painful eye with haloes, a fixed mid-dilated oval pupil and vomiting — needs same-day pressure-lowering to save the eye (see acute angle-closure glaucoma). A chemical burn (especially alkali) needs immediate copious irrigation before anything else. Suspected penetrating globe injury — shield the eye, do not press. Contact-lens wearers and the HSV dendritic ulcer mean sight-threatening keratitis (see HSV keratitis) — and never give topical steroids to an undiagnosed red eye (they turn a dendritic ulcer into a blinding geographic one). Orbital cellulitis (proptosis, painful restricted movements, fever) is a life-threatening emergency (see proptosis).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Acute angle-closure glaucoma
  • Red painful eye + haloes + blurred vision + nausea / vomiting; a hard globe
  • Fixed, mid-dilated, oval pupil; hazy cornea — often an elderly, long-sighted patient in dim light (see acute angle-closure glaucoma)
  • Same-day IOP-lowering + pilocarpine → laser iridotomy
🚩Cornea & orbit emergencies
  • Microbial keratitis / corneal ulcer — contact-lens wearers; the HSV dendritic ulcer (fluorescein) (see HSV keratitis)
  • Chemical burn (esp. alkali) → irrigate immediately; penetrating globe injury → shield, do not press
  • Orbital cellulitis — proptosis, painful restricted eye movements, fever (see proptosis)
🟠Anterior uveitis / iritis
  • Aching red eye + photophobia (including consensual) + watering; vision mildly reduced
  • Circumcorneal (ciliary) flush, small / irregular pupil, cells ± hypopyon on slit-lamp (see uveitis / iritis)
  • Look for a systemic association (HLA-B27, sarcoid, IBD); treat with steroid + cycloplegic
🟠Conjunctivitis
  • Bacterial — purulent discharge, lids stuck in the morning, gritty
  • Viral — watery, follicles, preauricular node, contagious; allergic — bilateral itch (see bacterial, allergic)
  • Comfortable eye, normal vision, reactive pupil — the reassuring pattern
🩹Scleritis vs episcleritis
  • Scleritis — severe boring pain (wakes from sleep), deep violaceous vessels that do not blanch with phenylephrine (see scleritis / episcleritis)
  • Often systemic vasculitis / connective tissue disease (e.g. RA, GPA) — can perforate
  • Episcleritis — mild, sectoral, comfortable, blanches with phenylephrine; self-limiting
🩹Benign & other
  • Subconjunctival haemorrhage — painless, flat red patch, normal vision; check BP / anticoagulation
  • Dry eye / blepharitis — grittiness, crusted lid margins, worse through the day
  • Foreign body / abrasion — sudden sharp pain; evert the lid and stain with fluorescein
Pain, vision and photophobia are the triage. A painful red eye, reduced vision or true photophobia means a dangerous cause (glaucoma, keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, orbital cellulitis). A comfortable eye with normal vision and discharge is almost always conjunctivitis. Never steroid an undiagnosed red eye.

OPHTHALMIC__Acute Painful Visual Loss:
Acute painful visual loss is an ophthalmic emergency — pain plus falling vision means the eye, optic nerve or a systemic vasculitis is under threat.
  • Two diagnoses must never be missed. In anyone over 50, sudden visual loss with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and a raised ESR / CRP is giant cell arteritis (arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy) (see giant cell arteritis, jaw claudication) — give high-dose steroids immediately to save the other eye.
  • A red, hard, painful eye with haloes and vomiting is acute angle-closure glaucoma (see acute angle-closure glaucoma). In a younger patient, pain on eye movement with reduced colour vision and an RAPD is optic neuritis (often demyelinating) (see multiple sclerosis, RAPD).
  • Surface causes — microbial keratitis / corneal ulcer (see keratitis), anterior uveitis (see uveitis), scleritis (see scleritis) and endophthalmitis — all present with a painful red eye (see red eye). Painless loss has a different list (see painless visual loss).
🚨Do not miss giant cell arteritis. Any patient over 50 with acute visual loss — especially with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or a swollen pale optic disc — has GCA until proven otherwise. Check ESR and CRP urgently and start high-dose corticosteroids the same day (do not wait for temporal artery biopsy) to protect the fellow eye (see giant cell arteritis). Acute angle-closure glaucoma (hard red eye, haloes, fixed mid-dilated pupil, vomiting) needs emergency IOP-lowering (see acute angle-closure glaucoma). Optic neuritis (pain on movement + RAPD + reduced colour vision) needs urgent neuro-ophthalmology and MRI. Endophthalmitis (recent surgery / intravitreal injection + pain + hypopyon + falling vision) is a blinding emergency needing an urgent vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics.

🚩Giant cell arteritis (arteritic AION)
  • Age >50 + headache + jaw claudication + scalp tenderness + malaise; pale swollen optic disc
  • Raised ESR / CRP — the fellow eye is at imminent risk (see giant cell arteritis, jaw claudication)

  • Hard red painful eye + haloes + blurred vision + vomiting
  • Fixed mid-dilated oval pupil, hazy cornea, very high IOP (see acute angle-closure glaucoma)
  • Emergency IOP-lowering + pilocarpine → laser iridotomy
🟠Optic neuritis
  • Pain on eye movement + subacute visual loss over hours–days; young adult (often female)
  • Reduced colour vision (red desaturation), RAPD; disc normal (retrobulbar) or swollen (see multiple sclerosis, RAPD)
  • Urgent MRI (demyelination); IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery
🟠Keratitis / corneal ulcer / endophthalmitis
  • Microbial keratitis — contact-lens wearers; the HSV dendritic ulcer (see HSV keratitis)
  • Endophthalmitis — recent surgery / intravitreal injection + pain + hypopyon + falling vision
  • Urgent scrape / vitreous tap + intensive antimicrobials; never steroid blindly
🩹Anterior uveitis
  • Aching red eye + photophobia + watering, mildly reduced vision
  • Ciliary flush, small / irregular pupil, cells ± hypopyon (see uveitis / iritis)
  • Look for a systemic association; steroid + cycloplegic
🩹Scleritis
  • Severe boring pain (wakes from sleep) + reduced vision; deep vessels not blanching (see scleritis / episcleritis)
  • Posterior scleritis can cause visual loss without obvious redness
  • Often systemic vasculitis / connective tissue disease; can perforate

OPHTHALMIC__Acute Painless Visual Loss:
Sudden painless loss of vision in a white eye is a vascular / retinal emergency until proven otherwise. The speed and pattern narrow it fast.
  • Instant, profound, monocular loss with an RAPD and a cherry-red spot is a central retinal artery occlusion (see CRAO) — a “stroke of the eye”: act as fast as possible and always exclude giant cell arteritis in the over-50s (see giant cell arteritis, jaw claudication).
  • Sudden loss with widespread retinal haemorrhages and engorged veins is a central retinal vein occlusion (see CRVO). Flashes, a shower of floaters and a curtain spreading across the field is a retinal detachment (see retinal detachment, flashes & floaters).
  • A sudden loss of the red reflex with floaters, often diabetic, is a vitreous haemorrhage (see diabetic retinopathy). Rapid central distortion in the elderly is wet AMD (see age-related macular degeneration, metamorphopsia); a homonymous field loss points to stroke (see stroke).
🚨Central retinal artery occlusion is a stroke of the eye — and giant cell arteritis can cause it. Sudden, profound, painless monocular loss with an RAPD, a pale retina and a cherry-red spot is a CRAO (see CRAO): irreversible retinal damage occurs from ~90–240 minutes, so attempt ocular massage / IOP-lowering and refer emergently, and treat it as a TIA / stroke equivalent with an urgent stroke pathway (carotid, ECG, risk factors) (see stroke / TIA). In anyone over 50, check ESR / CRP and start high-dose steroids if GCA is suspected to save the fellow eye (see giant cell arteritis). A curtain with flashes and floaters is a retinal detachment — same-day ophthalmology before the macula detaches (see retinal detachment). Wet AMD needs urgent anti-VEGF (see wet AMD).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Central retinal artery occlusion
  • Instant, profound, painless monocular loss + RAPD; pale retina with a cherry-red spot
  • A “stroke of the eye” — exclude giant cell arteritis (over-50s, ESR / CRP) (see CRAO, giant cell arteritis)
  • Act immediately (ocular massage / IOP-lowering) + urgent stroke pathway (see stroke / TIA)
🚩Retinal detachment
  • Flashes + shower of floaters + a curtain / shadow spreading across the field (see retinal detachment, flashes & floaters)
  • Macula-on (central vision spared) = save it today; macula-off is a worse prognosis
  • Risk: myopia, trauma, previous detachment, posterior vitreous detachment
🟠Central retinal vein occlusion
  • Sudden painless loss, less profound than CRAO; often on waking
  • Stormy-sunset fundus — widespread retinal haemorrhages, engorged tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots (see CRVO)
  • Risk: hypertension, glaucoma, hyperviscosity; watch for neovascular complications
🟠Wet (neovascular) AMD
  • Rapid central visual loss + distortion (metamorphopsia) in an elderly patient
  • Choroidal neovascular membrane — macular haemorrhage / fluid on OCT (see age-related macular degeneration, metamorphopsia)
  • Urgent anti-VEGF can preserve vision — refer fast
🩹Vitreous haemorrhage
  • Sudden floaters / haze / loss with a reduced or absent red reflex and no view of the fundus
  • Commonest cause is proliferative diabetic retinopathy; also retinal tear / detachment (see diabetic retinopathy)
  • B-scan if no fundal view; treat the underlying cause
🩹Stroke / cortical visual loss
  • Homonymous field defect (respecting the vertical midline) ± other neurology (see stroke / TIA)
  • Binocular; acuity may be normal — it is a field, not an eye, problem
  • Activate the stroke pathway — urgent brain imaging
Speed, the RAPD and the fundus sort it. Instant + RAPD + cherry-red spot = CRAO (exclude GCA, treat as a stroke); curtain + flashes / floaters = detachment; widespread haemorrhages = CRVO; central distortion = wet AMD; field defect = stroke.

OPHTHALMIC__Gradual Visual Loss:
Gradual, painless visual loss is usually chronic eye disease — but one cause is silently blinding and a few are sinister.
  • The four big diagnoses of age are cataract (gradual blur, glare and haloes, a myopic shift, an absent red reflex) (see cataracts), chronic open-angle glaucoma (see open-angle glaucoma), age-related macular degeneration (see AMD) and the vascular retinopathies of diabetes and hypertension (see diabetic, hypertensive retinopathy).
  • Open-angle glaucoma is the one that quietly steals peripheral vision — painless, symptomless until late, and irreversible, which is why screening the pressure, disc and fields matters.
  • Do not label everything “old age”: a gradual bitemporal field loss is a compressive / pituitary lesion (see bitemporal hemianopia, brain tumour), and new distortion on a chronic background is wet AMD (see metamorphopsia). Much “loss” is simply refractive error — correctable with glasses.
🚨Chronic open-angle glaucoma blinds silently and irreversibly. It is painless and symptomless until advanced, taking peripheral vision first, so it is caught by screening — raised IOP, a cupped optic disc and arcuate field defects (see chronic open-angle glaucoma). Treatment halts, but cannot reverse, the damage. Two red flags must not be dismissed as ageing: a gradual bitemporal hemianopia is a compressive lesion at the chiasm (pituitary tumour) needing MRI (see bitemporal hemianopia, brain tumour), and new distortion — straight lines suddenly wavy — signals wet AMD and urgent anti-VEGF (see wet AMD, metamorphopsia). And in a child, an absent red reflex / leukocoria is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise (see leukocoria).

🚩Chronic open-angle glaucoma
  • Silent, painless, symptomless until late — takes peripheral vision first; the damage is irreversible
  • Raised IOP, a cupped optic disc (↑cup:disc ratio) and arcuate field defects (see chronic open-angle glaucoma)
  • Caught by screening; treat to lower IOP (drops / laser / surgery) to halt progression
🚩Sinister mimics — do not call it “old age”
  • Bitemporal hemianopia — a compressive lesion at the chiasm (pituitary tumour) → MRI (see bitemporal hemianopia, brain tumour)
  • New distortion on a chronic background = wet AMD → urgent anti-VEGF (see metamorphopsia)
  • Slowly progressive loss with optic atrophy / an RAPD = compressive optic neuropathy (see RAPD)
🟠Cataract
  • Gradual painless blur, glare and haloes (especially night driving), colours faded
  • Myopic shift (“second sight”), absent / dim red reflex, lens opacity on slit-lamp (see cataracts)
  • Very treatable — day-case phacoemulsification with lens implant
🟠Age-related macular degeneration
  • Gradual central visual loss and difficulty reading / recognising faces; peripheral vision spared

OPHTHALMIC__Diplopia:
Approached through the eye and orbit, diplopia splits first into monocular and binocular.
  • Cover one eye: if the double vision persists it is monocular — an ocular problem (cataract, astigmatism, dry eye, dislocated lens), corrected by refraction, not neurology (see cataracts). If it resolves, it is binocular — the eyes are misaligned, from an orbital (restrictive), cranial-nerve or neuromuscular cause.
  • The commonest restrictive cause is thyroid eye disease (proptosis + lid retraction + restricted elevation) (see thyroid eye disease, proptosis); the nerve palsies are III, IV and VI (see cranial nerve palsies); and fatigable diplopia with ptosis is myasthenia gravis (see myasthenia, ptosis).
  • The red flag is a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil — a posterior communicating artery aneurysm (see aneurysm, abnormal pupils). For the wider neurological framing, see diplopia (neurological).
🚨A painful, pupil-involving third nerve palsy is an aneurysm until proven otherwise. A down-and-out eye with ptosis and a fixed dilated pupil, especially if painful, is a compressive posterior communicating artery aneurysm — image the vessels urgently (CT / CT angiography) before it ruptures (see intracranial aneurysm / haemorrhage, cranial nerve palsies). Proptosis with painful ophthalmoplegia, chemosis and fever is orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis (see proptosis, cavernous sinus thrombosis). An isolated sixth nerve palsy can be a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure (see raised ICP), and new diplopia in the over-50s with headache / jaw claudication may be giant cell arteritis (see giant cell arteritis).

OPHTHALMIC__Proptosis:
Proptosis is forward displacement of the globe — the question is whether it is the common, chronic thyroid eye disease or a dangerous orbital emergency.
  • Note the tempo and laterality: bilateral and gradual is usually thyroid eye disease (lid retraction, lid lag, restricted elevation), the commonest cause (see thyroid eye disease, exophthalmos).
  • Acute, painful, unilateral proptosis with fever and restricted, painful movements is orbital cellulitis — a sight- and life-threatening emergency, usually spreading from the sinuses (see sinusitis). Slowly progressive, unilateral proptosis with a mass suggests an orbital tumour (lymphoma, meningioma, metastasis; rhabdomyosarcoma in a child) (see orbital tumour).
  • Cavernous sinus pathology — thrombosis (painful ophthalmoplegia, chemosis, often bilateral) or a carotid-cavernous fistula (pulsatile proptosis + bruit + corkscrew vessels) — is the other danger (see cavernous sinus thrombosis). Always assess the optic nerve — a compressed nerve is a sight-threatening emergency (see diplopia).
🚨Acute painful proptosis with fever is orbital cellulitis until proven otherwise. Proptosis + painful, restricted eye movements + reduced acuity / colour vision + chemosis + fever (often after sinusitis) is a sight- and life-threatening orbital cellulitis — get an urgent CT of the orbit and sinuses, bloods and IV antibiotics, and watch for abscess and intracranial spread (see sinusitis). Cavernous sinus thrombosis spreads to the fellow eye with painful ophthalmoplegia and chemosis (see cavernous sinus thrombosis). In any proptosis, a relative afferent pupillary defect, reduced colour vision or a swollen disc signals compressive optic neuropathy — including from severe thyroid eye disease — and needs emergency decompression. A pulsatile proptosis with a bruit is a carotid-cavernous fistula.

OPHTHALMIC__Watery / Discharging Eye:
A watery or discharging eye is usually conjunctivitis or a blocked tear duct — but the character of the discharge and the age of the patient flag the dangerous few.
  • Purulent discharge with lids stuck together is bacterial conjunctivitis (see bacterial conjunctivitis); watery discharge with follicles and a tender preauricular node is viral; bilateral itch with stringy discharge is allergic (see allergic conjunctivitis).
  • The red flags: a neonate with a purulent eye is ophthalmia neonatorum — gonococcal (hyperacute, sight-threatening) or chlamydial (see gonococcal, chlamydial, associated STI); an adult with hyperacute copious purulent discharge is gonococcal and can perforate the cornea.
  • A painful, photophobic, watery red eye is keratitis (see HSV keratitis, red eye). Constant watering without discharge (epiphora) is usually a nasolacrimal drainage problem or reflex tearing from surface irritation.
🚨A neonate or an adult with hyperacute copious purulent discharge is an emergency. The same picture in an adult is gonococcal until proven otherwise. A painful, photophobic, watery red eye — especially a contact-lens wearer or a fluorescein-staining dendritic ulcer — is sight-threatening keratitis (see HSV keratitis). In an infant, watering + photophobia + an enlarged, cloudy cornea is congenital glaucoma — refer the same day. And a hot, tender swelling at the medial canthus is acute dacryocystitis.

OPHTHALMIC__Flashes & Floaters:
Flashes and floaters are common and usually a benign posterior vitreous detachment — but the same symptoms herald a sight-threatening retinal tear or detachment, so every new case needs a dilated fundal examination.
  • As the vitreous liquefies and pulls away with age, it tugs on the retina (flashes, photopsia) and casts shadows (floaters) — a posterior vitreous detachment, which is harmless in itself but can tear the retina (see posterior vitreous detachment / retinal detachment).
  • The red flags that a tear or retinal detachment has occurred are a sudden shower of many new floaters, persistent flashes, a curtain or shadow spreading across the field, and reduced vision or an RAPD (see retinal detachment, RAPD).
  • A sudden crop of floaters with a lost red reflex in a diabetic is a vitreous haemorrhage (see diabetic retinopathy); floaters with blurring and inflammation suggest posterior uveitis / vitritis (see uveitis). Bilateral zig-zag lights are usually migraine aura (see migraine), not the retina.
🚨New flashes and floaters are a retinal detachment until a dilated exam says otherwise. The warning symptoms are a sudden shower of new floaters, persistent or increasing flashes, and a dark curtain or shadow advancing across the visual field — refer for same-day dilated fundoscopy to find and treat a tear before the macula detaches (see retinal detachment, painless visual loss). Once central vision drops or there is an RAPD, the macula is threatened and surgery is urgent. Higher risk: myopia, trauma, previous detachment / surgery, aphakia. A sudden burst of floaters with a reduced red reflex is a vitreous haemorrhage (see diabetic retinopathy), and a “shower of black dots” with vitreous cells can be posterior uveitis — both still need urgent assessment.

OPHTHALMIC__Relative Afferent Pupillary:
A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, or Marcus Gunn pupil) is the single most useful objective sign of optic nerve or extensive retinal disease.
  • On the swinging-light test, both pupils constrict less — and paradoxically dilate — when the light swings to the affected eye, because that eye conducts less afferent signal to the brainstem. It localises to the optic nerve or a large retinal lesion, never to a media opacity: a dense cataract or refractive error does not cause an RAPD.
  • The causes to know are optic neuritis (see optic neuritis / MS), ischaemic optic neuropathy — including arteritic AION from giant cell arteritis (see giant cell arteritis, jaw claudication), a central retinal artery occlusion (see CRAO), an extensive retinal detachment (see retinal detachment), an ischaemic CRVO (see CRVO), and compressive or advanced glaucomatous optic neuropathy (see compressive lesion, glaucoma).
  • An RAPD is a red flag: pair it with the visual history (see painless, painful visual loss).
🚨An RAPD means the optic nerve or a large part of the retina is damaged — find the cause urgently. In anyone over 50 with an RAPD and a pale, swollen optic disc, assume arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy from giant cell arteritis — check ESR / CRP and start high-dose steroids the same day to save the fellow eye (see giant cell arteritis). An RAPD with instant profound loss and a cherry-red spot is a CRAO — a stroke of the eye (see CRAO). An RAPD with pain on eye movement and red desaturation in a young patient is optic neuritis — image for demyelination (see multiple sclerosis). A new RAPD with a gradual history can mean a compressive lesion squeezing the optic nerve or chiasm (see tumour) — do not attribute it to cataract, which never causes an RAPD.

OPHTHALMIC__Amaurosis Fugax (Transient V:
Amaurosis fugax — a transient, painless curtain of visual loss that fully recovers — is a warning shot, not a benign event.
  • Classic amaurosis fugax is a transient monocular loss lasting seconds to minutes, described as a curtain descending and lifting, caused by an embolus from the carotid — it is a transient ischaemic attack and a marker of imminent stroke, so it enters the urgent TIA pathway (see TIA / stroke).
  • The other emergency is giant cell arteritis: transient visual loss in the over-50s with headache, jaw claudication or a raised ESR heralds permanent blindness — do not miss it (see giant cell arteritis, jaw claudication). Consider a cardioembolic source (see atrial fibrillation) and ocular hypoperfusion from tight carotid stenosis.
  • Not every transient loss is embolic: brief postural visual obscurations with papilloedema point to raised intracranial pressure / IIH (see idiopathic intracranial hypertension), and stereotyped scintillations are retinal / ocular migraine (see migraine). A loss that does not recover is an occlusion (see painless visual loss).
🚨Transient visual loss is a TIA or giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise — both are emergencies. A transient monocular curtain is a TIA: assess and image urgently (same-day / next-day TIA clinic), give aspirin, and arrange carotid imaging, an ECG and vascular risk-factor control — a tight symptomatic carotid stenosis needs prompt endarterectomy to prevent stroke (see TIA / stroke). In anyone over 50, transient visual loss with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or a raised ESR / CRP is giant cell arteritis — a true emergency that will blind the eye (and then the other) if untreated: check ESR / CRP and start high-dose steroids the same day (see giant cell arteritis). Transient obscurations with papilloedema signal raised intracranial pressure and need urgent imaging (see raised ICP).

OPHTHALMIC__Visual Distortion (Metamorph:
Metamorphopsia — straight lines looking wavy or bent, with objects the wrong size — is the signature of macular disease, and it demands an urgent macula assessment.
  • Distortion means the photoreceptors of the fovea have been displaced by fluid, blood, a membrane or traction, so the map on the retina is buckled.
  • The emergency is wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration — new distortion with a central scotoma in an older patient means a choroidal neovascular membrane that needs urgent anti-VEGF to save central vision (see wet AMD). Macular oedema is the other big cause — from diabetes (see diabetic maculopathy) or a retinal vein occlusion (see CRVO).
  • More slowly, an epiretinal membrane, a macular hole or central serous chorioretinopathy distort the macula. The key tools are the Amsler grid and OCT. Distinguish true macular distortion from a transient migraine shimmer (see migraine); a sudden central loss goes down the urgent pathway (see painless visual loss, gradual visual loss).
🚨New metamorphopsia is wet AMD until the macula is imaged — refer urgently. In an older patient, sudden distortion (straight lines wavy) with a central scotoma signals a choroidal neovascular membrane of wet age-related macular degeneration; prompt anti-VEGF (within days) can preserve central vision, so this is an urgent macula referral, not a routine one (see wet AMD). Give patients at risk an Amsler grid to self-monitor and to return immediately if lines distort. Diabetic macular oedema is a leading cause of visual loss in working-age adults and also needs prompt treatment (see diabetic maculopathy); macular oedema from a vein occlusion behaves similarly (see CRVO). The reassuring pattern — a young or middle-aged patient with central distortion, micropsia and a small central “dark disc” — is often central serous chorioretinopathy, which is usually self-limiting.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Wet (neovascular) AMD
  • New distortion (straight lines wavy) + a central scotoma in an older patient
  • A choroidal neovascular membrane — macular fluid / haemorrhage on OCT (see age-related macular degeneration)
  • Urgent anti-VEGF (within days) preserves vision — an urgent macula referral
🚩Macular oedema (diabetic / vein occlusion)
  • Diabetic macular oedema — distortion + central blur; a leading cause of working-age visual loss (see diabetic maculopathy)
  • Macular oedema from a vein occlusion (CRVO / BRVO) causes distortion + reduced central vision (see CRVO)
  • Both need prompt macular assessment and treatment (anti-VEGF / laser)
🟠Central serous chorioretinopathy
  • Young / middle-aged man, often stress / steroids / type-A; central distortion + micropsia + a dim central patch
  • Serous neurosensory detachment (subretinal fluid) at the macula on OCT
  • Usually self-limiting — stop steroids; refer if persistent
🟠Epiretinal membrane / vitreomacular traction
  • Gradual distortion + mildly reduced acuity; a cellophane macular sheen (macular pucker)
  • Contractile membrane / traction wrinkling the macula on OCT
  • Observe if mild; vitrectomy + membrane peel if visually significant
🩹Macular hole
  • Central distortion progressing to a central grey / black spot (a central scotoma)
  • A full-thickness foveal defect on OCT; positive Watzke–Allen sign
  • Surgical repair (vitrectomy) for full-thickness holes
🩹How to assess & what is NOT the macula
  • Amsler grid (wavy / missing lines) + OCT are the key tests; every case is a macula referral (see gradual visual loss)
  • A transient shimmering / zig-zag that marches and fades is migraine, not macular (see migraine)
  • A sudden central loss goes down the urgent visual-loss pathway (see painless visual loss)
Distortion = the macula; new distortion = wet AMD until imaged. Screen with an Amsler grid, confirm with OCT, and refer urgently — anti-VEGF is time-critical for wet AMD and macular oedema. A marching shimmer that fades is migraine.

3Assess & act
At the bedside — acuity, the Amsler grid, dilated macular fundoscopy
History & red flags
Onset and tempo (sudden = wet AMD; gradual = membrane / hole), age, diabetes and glycaemic control, a prior vein occlusion, steroid use / stress (CSCR), micropsia / macropsia, a central scotoma; distinguish a persistent macular distortion from a transient migraine shimmer
Examine
Visual acuity + the Amsler grid (map the wavy / missing area), dilated fundoscopy of the macula (haemorrhage / fluid / drusen; cellophane sheen; a foveal hole), and check the fellow eye; an RAPD is usually absent in isolated macular disease
Investigate
OCT of the macula is the key test (subretinal / intraretinal fluid, a neovascular membrane, an epiretinal membrane, a full-thickness hole); fluorescein angiography (± OCT-angiography) for a choroidal neovascular membrane / leakage; glucose / HbA1c and blood pressure for oedema
Act
Wet AMD → urgent anti-VEGF (time-critical); diabetic / vein-occlusion macular oedema → anti-VEGF / laser + optimise diabetes / BP; CSCR → stop steroids, observe (treat if persistent); epiretinal membrane / macular hole → vitrectomy ± peel if significant; give an Amsler grid to self-monitor the fellow eye

The rules that carry it: distortion means the macula. New metamorphopsia is wet AMD until an OCT says otherwise — refer urgently for anti-VEGF. Diabetic / vein-occlusion oedema also needs prompt treatment; a young man with micropsia is usually CSCR.
